questions.scenario: Your Microsoft Entra tenant contains a user named User1. User1 must be able to create and manage groups, but must not receive broader directory administration rights.
questions.stem: Which role should you assign to User1?
questions.subtopic: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
questions.hint: Consider least privilege: which role's scope covers ONLY group management without overlapping user administration or security tasks?

options.rationale: This role can manage users and groups, which is broader than the stated requirement.
This role can create and manage groups without adding unrelated tenant-wide permissions.
This role is intended for security posture and policy tasks, not day-to-day group administration.
This role grants full directory control and violates least privilege.

questions.explanation: Groups Administrator is the least-privileged built-in role that covers creating and managing Microsoft Entra groups.

questions.scenario: You are piloting self-service password reset (SSPR). Only members of the Finance-Pilot security group should be able to use SSPR during the first phase.
questions.stem: Which SSPR configuration should you choose?
questions.subtopic: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
questions.hint: In a pilot scenario, you need to target a SPECIFIC GROUP for rollout. Which SSPR scope allows group-based eligibility?

options.rationale: This exposes the feature to every user instead of only the pilot population.
This lets you target the pilot group and expand later if the rollout is successful.

options.text: Enable SSPR for guest users only
options.rationale: Guest-only scope does not meet the requirement for internal finance employees.

options.text: Disable SSPR and use Conditional Access
options.rationale: Conditional Access does not enable password reset workflows.

questions.explanation: SSPR supports targeted rollout to selected groups, which is the standard way to pilot the feature before enabling it tenant-wide.

questions.scenario: External auditors must access Azure resources by using their existing business email accounts. You want to avoid creating separate cloud-only accounts for them.
questions.stem: Which identity object should you use for the auditors?
questions.subtopic: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
questions.hint: The requirement is to avoid creating NEW cloud accounts. Which identity type lets external users sign in with their EXISTING home organization credentials?

options.rationale: B2B guest users can be invited by email and authenticated with their existing identity provider.
Managed identities are for workloads, not people signing in interactively.
Service principals represent applications, not external auditors.
This would create separate accounts and does not preserve the auditors' existing identities.

questions.explanation: Guest users are the correct way to provide B2B access while allowing external auditors to sign in with existing identities.

questions.scenario: An operations team must start, stop, and redeploy virtual machines in the RG-App resource group. They must not manage RBAC assignments or modify unrelated resources in the subscription.
questions.stem: Which built-in Azure role should you assign at RG-App?
questions.hint: Filter for roles that cover VM operations (start, stop, deploy) WITHOUT including resource group management or RBAC administration rights.

options.rationale: Reader cannot start or stop virtual machines.
This role manages access assignments rather than virtual machine operations.
This role is scoped to virtual machine management tasks without granting user access administration rights.
Contributor can manage most resources in the resource group, which is broader than the requirement.

questions.explanation: Virtual Machine Contributor grants the required VM management permissions without the broad resource control of Contributor.

questions.scenario: An operations engineer is onboarded with Reader at the subscription scope and Contributor on RG-Dev only. The engineer must deploy, update, and delete test resources in RG-Dev during a two-week validation window, but must not gain permission to manage RBAC, and must not be able to change workloads in RG-Prod or RG-Shared. There are no deny assignments or custom roles.
questions.stem: What access does the engineer actually have in RG-Dev and outside it?
questions.hint: Effective access is ADDITIVE across scopes. Contributor at RG-Dev permits WRITE operations within that scope. What actual operations does that enable vs restrict?

options.text: The engineer can create and manage resources only in RG-Dev
options.rationale: Contributor at the resource-group scope allows management in that group, while subscription-level Reader remains read-only elsewhere.

options.text: The engineer can create resources in every resource group in the subscription
options.rationale: Reader at the subscription scope does not grant write access outside RG-Dev.

options.text: The engineer can only view resources in RG-Dev
options.rationale: Contributor overrides the read-only assignment within RG-Dev for management operations.

options.text: The engineer can assign roles in RG-Dev
options.rationale: Contributor does not include RBAC role assignment rights.

questions.explanation: Effective access is additive and scope-bound: Contributor at RG-Dev allows write operations only inside that resource group, while subscription-level Reader still applies outside RG-Dev. Neither assignment grants RBAC administration rights (User Access Administrator). Role combinations follow the principle of highest-privilege-at-any-scope.

questions.scenario: The platform team deploys resources through several pipelines into a landing zone that must always carry a CostCenter tag. New deployments should continue even when the tag is missing, but the governance rule also needs to backfill existing resources that were created before the standard was introduced.
questions.stem: Which Azure governance feature should you use to satisfy both requirements without blocking deployment?
questions.hint: You need to ADD tags during deployment AND fix existing resources later. Which policy effect can do BOTH through deployment and remediation?

options.text: Azure Policy with the Modify effect
options.rationale: Modify can add or fix tag values during deployment, and remediation can bring existing resources into compliance.
Locks prevent changes or deletion, but they do not add metadata to resources.
Budgets track spend and alerts, but they do not alter resource properties.
Management groups provide hierarchy, but they do not directly enforce or add tags.

questions.explanation: The Modify effect in Azure Policy can add or correct tag values as resources are deployed, and remediation can bring older resources into compliance later.

questions.scenario: A production resource group contains customer-facing workloads and is entering a change freeze before quarter-end reporting. The operations team must prevent accidental deletion of the resource group itself, but administrators still need to scale, patch, and update resources inside the group without opening a change window for every routine edit.
questions.stem: Which lock should you apply to the resource group to meet both requirements?
questions.hint: Distinguish between lock types: ReadOnly blocks ALL writes (updates/patches), while CanNotDelete blocks only deletion. Which allows routine operations?

options.rationale: ReadOnly would also block routine changes such as scaling and patching.
CanNotDelete blocks accidental deletion while still allowing legitimate updates inside the resource group.
Audit records noncompliance but does not prevent deletion.
Budgets are for cost management, not resource protection.

questions.explanation: CanNotDelete lock is the appropriate governance control for this scenario. It blocks deletion of the resource group itself (which is the accidental deletion risk) but still permits all write operations (scaling, patching, updates) inside the group. ReadOnly would block writes and violate the operational requirement.

questions.scenario: The finance division has eight Azure subscriptions spread across three regions. Security and compliance teams must apply the same policy assignments and inherited RBAC access once at a parent scope while each subscription still keeps its own workload-specific resource groups and local deployment pipelines without being flattened into a single structure.
questions.stem: At which Azure scope should you organize the finance subscriptions so governance flows down without changing the workload layout?
questions.hint: You have 8 subscriptions across multiple regions. At what SCOPE can you apply governance so it flows down to all child subscriptions automatically?

options.rationale: Management groups let you apply governance and role assignments above the subscription level.
Resource groups exist inside a single subscription and cannot contain other subscriptions.
Virtual networks are networking resources, not governance containers.
Budgets do not provide inheritance for policy or RBAC.

questions.explanation: Management groups provide the required hierarchy when the same governance settings must flow to multiple subscriptions without flattening workload boundaries.

questions.scenario: A development subscription needs an alert when monthly spend reaches 80 percent of forecast so the team can review usage before month end. The alert must be informational only, should not pause deployments, and must work without introducing any governance control that could affect the application's release pipeline.
questions.stem: Which feature should you configure?
questions.referenceTopic: Manage costs by using alerts and budgets
questions.hint: The alert must be informational only and NOT block deployments. Which feature sends threshold-based notifications without enforcement?

options.rationale: Service Health tracks Microsoft service events, not subscription spending.
Locks do not provide spending notifications and would disrupt deployments.
Management groups are organizational, not spend-threshold alerting tools.

options.text: A budget with an alert threshold
options.rationale: Budgets are designed to monitor spend and trigger alerts at defined thresholds.

questions.explanation: Budgets can trigger notifications at custom cost thresholds without enforcing a deployment stop or changing deployment behavior.

questions.scenario: Leadership wants a native Azure service that can surface underutilized virtual machines and disks, highlight cost-saving opportunities, and prioritize recommendations the operations team can act on before the next billing cycle ends. The team has a small staff, cannot add a third-party optimization platform, must keep the workflow lightweight, and wants guidance that improves cost without creating extra operational overhead.
questions.stem: Which Azure service should you review first to balance cost reduction with low operational overhead?
questions.referenceTopic: Manage costs by using Azure Advisor recommendations
questions.hint: Which NATIVE Azure service surfaces rightsizing recommendations and cost-saving opportunities without requiring third-party tools?

options.rationale: Advisor provides cost, reliability, security, operational excellence, and performance recommendations including rightsizing guidance.
The Activity Log records control-plane actions but does not recommend cost savings.
Policy evaluates compliance and can enforce rules, but it does not surface rightsizing recommendations.
Backup reports show protection posture rather than cost optimization guidance.

questions.explanation: Azure Advisor is the built-in service that surfaces rightsizing and cost optimization recommendations for Azure resources, including underutilized compute and storage.

questions.scenario: The identity team adds new hires to the Sales-Licensed group during onboarding and wants each member to receive Microsoft Entra ID P1 automatically. They must keep the licensing model maintainable as employees join and leave the group throughout the month without assigning licenses to each user one by one.
questions.stem: Which licensing approach should you use to meet this requirement?
questions.subtopic: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
questions.referenceTopic: Manage licenses in Microsoft Entra ID
questions.hint: Think about automation—when group membership changes, how can licenses follow automatically without manual work?

options.rationale: Group-based licensing automatically assigns licenses to current and future group members.
Direct assignments require manual work for every new user.
Administrative units scope administration but do not assign licenses.
Access reviews govern membership recertification, not licensing.

questions.explanation: Group-based licensing is the efficient, repeatable method when every member of a group must receive the same license set and the assignment should follow group membership automatically.

questions.scenario: The security team must stop anyone in a subscription from creating new public IP addresses. Existing public IP resources can remain in place for now, but the policy must block any new deployment attempts while leaving the current workloads untouched and without requiring manual cleanup.
questions.stem: Which Azure feature should you configure to enforce that requirement?
questions.hint: Which Azure feature can actively BLOCK resource creation attempts at deployment time without affecting existing resources?

options.text: Azure Policy with the Deny effect
options.rationale: Deny blocks noncompliant resource creation requests at deployment time.
A deletion lock does not stop new public IP resources from being created.
Advisor can recommend changes but cannot block deployments.
Budgets track spending and do not enforce resource-type restrictions.

questions.explanation: Azure Policy with a Deny effect is the correct control when new public IP deployments must be prevented while leaving already deployed resources alone.

questions.scenario: Contractors in the Storage-Ops security group must manage only the storage accounts in the RG-Finance resource group. The access model must stay narrow enough to avoid subscription-wide permissions, and the team wants to avoid managing individual user assignments one by one while still keeping the role assignment easy to maintain.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take to implement that access model? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.hint: Think about two pieces: First, what identity object simplifies RBAC management? Second, at what scope and with which role should you assign?

options.text: Assign the Storage Account Contributor role to the Storage-Ops group at the RG-Finance scope
options.rationale: This grants the needed storage management permissions only within the required resource group.

options.text: Assign the Owner role to the Storage-Ops group at the subscription scope
options.rationale: This is far broader than necessary and violates least privilege.

options.text: Create or use a security group for the contractors
options.rationale: Using a group simplifies RBAC management and aligns with the scenario.

options.text: Assign the Reader role at the tenant root group
options.rationale: Reader at the tenant root does not provide storage management permissions.

questions.explanation: The correct design is to manage access through a group and assign the minimum required role at the narrowest practical scope, which here is the RG-Finance resource group.

questions.scenario: Across all landing zone subscriptions, missing ownership tags must be added automatically while any attempt to deploy a public IP resource must be blocked. The governance design needs to stamp metadata on compliant resources and still prevent a risky resource type from being deployed without creating a separate manual tagging process.
questions.stem: Which two Azure Policy effects should you use to satisfy both outcomes while preserving deployment enforcement? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.hint: You need two effects: one to BLOCK creation of public IPs, another to ADD tags. Which pair handles both enforcement and tagging?

options.rationale: Audit reports noncompliance but does not block or correct the deployment.
Deny can block deployment of disallowed resource types such as public IP addresses.
Modify can add or adjust required tags and can be paired with remediation for existing resources.
Disabled turns off enforcement and does not solve either requirement.

questions.explanation: Deny and Modify are complementary: Deny blocks deployment of disallowed resource types (public IPs), while Modify adds or corrects tags during deployment. Using both effects together satisfies the dual requirement of enforcement (Deny) and automated tagging (Modify) without requiring separate manual processes.

questions.scenario: Finance wants a budget alert when monthly spend reaches 80 percent of budget, while a separate monthly review should surface cost-saving recommendations the team can act on before the next billing cycle. The solution must alert and advise, but it should not block deployments or force a governance change.
questions.stem: Which two Azure features should you use to meet both needs? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.referenceTopic: Manage costs by using alerts, budgets, and Azure Advisor recommendations
questions.hint: You need spending ALERTS and RECOMMENDATIONS. Which two services provide each without blocking deployments?

options.rationale: Budgets provide threshold-based cost notifications.
Resource locks do not provide cost controls or notifications.
Advisor provides cost-saving recommendations such as rightsizing guidance.
Activity Log alerts are event-driven and not designed for budget thresholds or cost recommendations.

questions.explanation: Budgets cover spend threshold notifications, while Azure Advisor is the native recommendation engine for cost optimization guidance. Together they satisfy alerting and monthly review without affecting deployments.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing proposed RBAC and governance statements for an Azure environment before a production rollout, and the team must avoid giving away overly broad permissions.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.hint: Test your knowledge of RBAC inheritance and permission models. Consider scope inheritance and what the Reader role actually permits.

statements.text: A role assignment created at the subscription scope is inherited by all resource groups in that subscription.
The Reader role lets a user delete a tag from a resource.

questions.explanation: RBAC assignments inherit from parent scopes. The Reader role does not allow write operations such as editing or removing tags.

questions.scenario: You are validating identity administration statements before a tenant rollout, and the rollout plan must support guest collaboration, scoped password reset, and group-based licensing without forcing a tenant-wide change.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.subtopic: Manage Microsoft Entra users and groups
questions.hint: Multi-statement validation: Can external users join groups? Can SSPR be scoped? Does licensing follow future members or only existing ones?

statements.text: Guest users can be added to Microsoft Entra groups.
Self-service password reset can be enabled for selected groups instead of the entire tenant.
Group-based licensing applies only to users who are already members at the time the license is assigned.

questions.explanation: Guest users can participate in group membership, SSPR can be rolled out to selected groups, and group-based licensing also applies to future group members.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing governance controls for a new landing zone that must protect production subscriptions, apply required tags to new resources, and provide budget notifications without blocking routine operations or forcing a separate change window for every update.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.referenceTopic: Implement and manage Azure Policy and resource locks
questions.hint: Validate lock and policy capabilities: What does ReadOnly actually block? Can Policy modify metadata? Do Budgets auto-shutdown resources?

statements.text: A ReadOnly lock prevents administrators from changing tags on a locked resource.
Azure Policy can append or modify tags during deployment.
A budget can automatically shut down virtual machines without any other automation component.

questions.explanation: ReadOnly locks block write operations, Azure Policy can stamp tags, and budgets alone only trigger notifications rather than performing shutdown actions.

questions.scenario: You are assigning a policy that must affect every subscription used by the finance division, but must not affect subscriptions owned by other divisions.
questions.stem: In the Azure portal hierarchy, which scope should you select?
questions.hint: At which SCOPE can you affect multiple subscriptions with a single policy assignment WITHOUT affecting other divisions?

options.rationale: A dedicated management group is the narrowest scope that can govern all finance subscriptions together.
A single subscription would not apply the policy to the other finance subscriptions.
A resource group is too low in the hierarchy and cannot contain subscriptions.
Tenant root would affect subscriptions outside the finance division.

questions.explanation: The finance management group is the correct scope because it captures all finance subscriptions without extending governance to unrelated divisions.

questions.scenario: A Modify policy for CostCenter tagging is already defined for a production landing zone. The policy must update existing resources that predate the assignment, while keeping compliant resources untouched and avoiding a rebuild of the environment.
questions.stem: Arrange the actions in the correct order so the policy can be applied and then remediated without rebuilding the environment or disrupting compliant resources.
questions.hint: Sequencing matters: What must EXIST before you can assign it? What must exist BEFORE you can remediate?
questions.explanation: The policy must exist before it can be assigned, and a remediation task is what applies the change to existing resources.

questions.scenario: A set of operators needs virtual machine management access through group-based RBAC, and the team must keep the deployment repeatable for future operators without reassigning the role one user at a time.
questions.stem: Arrange the actions in the correct order.
questions.hint: The group must exist BEFORE you can add users to it. Role assignment comes AFTER both group and membership exist.
availableItems: Assign the role at the resource group scope
Add the operators to the group
correctOrder: Add the operators to the group
Assign the role at the resource group scope
questions.explanation: Create the group first, place users into it, and then assign the role at the scope that needs to be controlled.

questions.scenario: A container stores rarely accessed archived product catalogs that must remain online for compliance audit purposes. The storage solution must incur the lowest possible monthly storage cost while meeting the 24-hour retrieval SLA for audit requests.
questions.stem: Which blob access tier should you use?
questions.subtopic: Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage
questions.hint: Balance cost vs availability: which tier stays ONLINE (not offline like Archive) but costs less than Hot?

options.rationale: Hot is optimized for frequent access and usually costs more to store.
Cool is optimized for infrequent access while keeping blobs available online.
Archive is offline and would not satisfy the requirement to keep data online.
Premium is for performance-sensitive workloads rather than low-cost infrequent access.

questions.explanation: The Cool tier is the lowest-cost online tier for infrequently accessed blob data.

questions.scenario: A storage account must replicate data to a paired region and allow read access to the replica during disaster recovery testing, while keeping the primary workload online and avoiding a separate reporting copy.
questions.stem: Which redundancy option should you choose to satisfy that requirement?
questions.hint: You need read access to the REPLICA. Which redundancy option includes '-RA-' for read-access?

options.rationale: GRS replicates to a paired region but does not provide read access to the secondary endpoint.
RA-GRS adds read access to the replicated secondary region endpoint.
ZRS protects within the primary region only and does not replicate to a second region.
LRS keeps copies in a single datacenter or region only.

questions.explanation: Read-access geo-redundant storage is specifically designed for regional replication plus read access to the secondary endpoint without changing how the primary endpoint is used.

questions.scenario: Subnet-App must access a storage account over the public endpoint, but traffic from all other networks must be blocked. You do not want to use private endpoints.
questions.stem: Which networking feature should you enable on Subnet-App?
questions.referenceTopic: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
questions.hint: Service endpoints vs private endpoints: Which keeps the PUBLIC endpoint in use but controls ACCESS by subnet?

options.rationale: Service endpoints let the subnet reach the storage account over the Azure backbone while still using the public endpoint.
Private endpoints use a private IP and are unnecessary when the public endpoint must remain in use.
Front Door is a global application delivery service, not a subnet-to-storage access control feature.
NAT gateway controls outbound internet translation, not storage firewall integration.

questions.explanation: Service endpoints are the correct subnet-side feature when the storage account should still be reached through its public endpoint but limited to selected virtual networks. You enable a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet-App, then configure the storage account firewall to allow traffic only from that service endpoint. This provides subnet-level access control while keeping the public endpoint active.

questions.scenario: An application uses a SAS token to upload blobs, and the operations team must be able to revoke that access without rotating the storage account keys or disrupting other workloads that share the same account.
questions.stem: What should you base the SAS token on to make revocation practical?
questions.hint: For revocation without key rotation, bind the SAS to what SERVER-SIDE control that can be modified independently?

options.rationale: Stored access policies let you change or remove the policy and invalidate dependent SAS tokens.
Key rotation is broader and affects every workload using that key.
Management groups do not participate in SAS token revocation.
Lifecycle rules manage blob data behavior, not authorization tokens.

questions.explanation: A stored access policy gives you a server-side control point for SAS lifetime and revocation without rotating account keys or affecting unrelated consumers of the account.

questions.scenario: You must script repeated uploads of 20 TB of file data from a Windows server to Azure Blob Storage, and the transfer process must be resumable, high-throughput, and suitable for unattended execution while minimizing manual cleanup after a network interruption.
questions.stem: Which tool should you use to meet those requirements?
questions.referenceTopic: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
questions.hint: Large scripted transfers with resume capability: which tool is built for unattended, high-throughput Azure Storage data movement?

options.rationale: Storage Explorer is useful interactively, but AzCopy is the better fit for large scripted transfers.
AzCopy is built for high-throughput scripted data movement into Azure Storage.
Portal uploads are not designed for repeated high-volume scripted transfers.
Advisor does not move data.

questions.explanation: AzCopy is the preferred tool for large, automated Azure Storage data transfer jobs because it supports high throughput and resumable transfers.

questions.scenario: Users on Windows servers joined to on-premises AD DS must access an Azure file share by using their existing domain credentials over SMB, and the storage account must support identity-based access without introducing guest accounts or shared passwords.
questions.stem: What should you configure on the storage account?
questions.referenceTopic: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
questions.hint: On-premises domain users need EXISTING credentials over SMB: which authentication method extends their identity into Azure Files?

options.rationale: Anonymous access does not apply to SMB access for Azure Files.

options.text: AD DS authentication for Azure Files
options.rationale: Azure Files can integrate with on-premises AD DS for identity-based SMB access.
SAS tokens do not provide traditional SMB identity-based domain authentication.
Public read access is unrelated to SMB access and is insecure for the scenario.

questions.explanation: When existing on-premises AD DS identities must authenticate over SMB, Azure Files should be configured for AD DS-based authentication.

questions.scenario: You plan to enable object replication between two storage accounts for block blobs, and the design must preserve version history while keeping the replication setup simple to operate later.
questions.stem: Which feature must be enabled first before you configure replication?
questions.hint: Object replication requires version tracking BEFORE setup: what server-side feature preserves blob history for replication?

options.rationale: Object replication relies on versioning to track changes between source and destination.
Soft delete is useful for recovery but is not the prerequisite for object replication.
NFS support is unrelated to blob replication.
Private connectivity is optional and not the replication prerequisite.

questions.explanation: Blob versioning is a core prerequisite for object replication between storage accounts and is required so changes can be tracked between source and destination.

questions.scenario: Security policy requires a storage account to use customer-managed keys (CMK) for encryption at rest, and the security team must keep key ownership in a dedicated service while avoiding any dependency on alerting or networking resources.
questions.stem: Which Azure service must host the encryption key to satisfy that requirement?
questions.hint: Customer-managed encryption keys must be stored in which dedicated Azure service? What keeps key ownership separate from alerting/networking?

options.rationale: Customer-managed keys for storage accounts are stored and managed in Key Vault.
Action groups handle alert actions and do not store encryption keys.
Stored access policies govern SAS permissions, not storage encryption.
Route tables control network traffic and are unrelated to encryption keys.

questions.explanation: Storage accounts that use CMK retrieve their encryption keys from Azure Key Vault, which is the dedicated key management service for this scenario.

questions.scenario: A support team frequently overwrites the same blobs by mistake during bulk data operations. Recovery must be possible without restoring the entire storage account or involving a third-party backup system, and the team's junior staff must be able to perform recovery without extensive training.
questions.stem: Which feature should you enable to make recovery straightforward?
questions.subtopic: Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage
questions.hint: Accidental overwrites need quick recovery without full account restore: what blob feature automatically keeps previous versions?

options.rationale: Versioning preserves previous blob versions when blobs are modified or overwritten.
Archive changes storage cost and retrieval behavior but does not retain overwritten versions.
Stored access policies affect authorization rather than data recovery.
File share snapshots apply to Azure Files, not blobs.

questions.explanation: Blob versioning is the direct feature used to recover prior blob contents after accidental overwrite operations.

questions.scenario: You need an automated rule that moves blobs to the Cool tier after 30 days and later deletes previous blob versions after 180 days, while keeping the storage account inexpensive to operate and preserving recoverability until the retention window closes. The storage team must avoid manual cleanup tasks and must keep the policy maintainable as the number of blobs grows.
questions.stem: Which two features should you configure to satisfy both parts of the policy? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Configure Azure Files and Azure Blob Storage
questions.referenceTopic: Configure blob lifecycle management and versioning
questions.hint: Two-step automation: Auto-move to Cool after 30 days AND delete versions after 180 days. Which two features provide both tiering actions and version cleanup?

options.rationale: Lifecycle management performs the automated tiering and deletion actions.
Versioning must be enabled so previous versions exist to be cleaned up later.
Premium performance does not create retention or lifecycle behavior.
SMB multichannel is unrelated to blob tier transitions or version cleanup.

questions.explanation: Lifecycle management provides the automation engine, and versioning is needed so there are prior versions to manage and eventually delete.

questions.scenario: Only servers in Subnet-App should reach a storage account over its public endpoint. Access from every other public network must be denied, while the public endpoint itself must remain available for the approved subnet.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take to enforce that design? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.referenceTopic: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
questions.hint: Keep public endpoint but restrict to ONE subnet only: which service endpoint feature pairs with firewall VNET rules?

options.text: Enable a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet-App
options.rationale: The subnet needs the service endpoint so Azure Storage firewall virtual network rules can be used.

options.text: Add Subnet-App as a virtual network rule in the storage account firewall
options.rationale: The storage firewall must explicitly trust the subnet.
A load balancer is unrelated to storage firewall access control.
Anonymous access weakens security and does not limit access to the subnet.

questions.explanation: Service endpoints and storage firewall virtual network rules are the paired controls when the public endpoint must stay in use but access must be restricted to selected subnets.

questions.scenario: An administrator must upload file content from a workstation into Azure Storage and wants two supported Microsoft tools that can handle both quick interactive uploads and scripted transfers without introducing third-party utilities.
questions.stem: Which two tools can you use? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.referenceTopic: Manage data by using Azure Storage Explorer and AzCopy
questions.hint: Two Microsoft tools for interactive AND scripted Azure Storage uploads: which provide both UI and CLI support?

options.rationale: Storage Explorer supports interactive upload, browse, and management for Azure Storage.
AzCopy supports command-line upload and download operations to Azure Storage.
Advisor provides recommendations and does not transfer files.
Service Health tracks incidents and maintenance events, not data transfer.

questions.explanation: Storage Explorer and AzCopy are both first-party tools built for Azure Storage data management and movement.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing storage access and resiliency statements for a landing zone design review, and you must verify which controls affect access revocation, redundancy, and recovery behavior without guessing.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.referenceTopic: Configure stored access policies and redundancy
questions.hint: Policy-based revocation vs regional redundancy vs blob recovery: distinguish access control from resiliency and recovery mechanisms.

statements.text: Deleting a stored access policy invalidates SAS tokens that depend on that policy.
Zone-redundant storage protects against a complete regional outage.
Blob soft delete helps recover deleted blobs for a defined retention period.

questions.explanation: Stored access policy removal revokes policy-based SAS tokens, ZRS stays within one region, and blob soft delete provides time-bound recovery for deleted blobs.

questions.scenario: You want an application to use a SAS token that you can later revoke without rotating storage account keys, and the process must remain easy to manage for future token updates.
questions.stem: Arrange the actions in the correct order so revocation stays possible later.
questions.hint: Revocable SAS tokens: What policy must exist FIRST, then be referenced in the token, then distributed to the app?
availableItems: Provide the SAS token to the application
Generate a SAS token that references the policy
correctOrder: Generate a SAS token that references the policy
Provide the SAS token to the application
questions.explanation: The policy must exist before a dependent SAS can be created and issued to the application.

questions.scenario: In the redundancy dropdown for a new storage account, you must choose protection across availability zones in the primary region and replication to a secondary region without giving up regional resiliency.
questions.stem: Which redundancy option should you select?
questions.hint: Zones in primary region PLUS secondary region replication: which redundancy option combines zonal protection with geo-replication?

options.rationale: LRS keeps copies in one region only and does not add zone or regional resilience.
ZRS protects across zones in the primary region but does not replicate to a secondary region.
GZRS combines zone protection in the primary region with geo-replication to a secondary region.
RA-GRS provides a readable secondary region but lacks primary-region zone redundancy.

questions.explanation: GZRS is the option that combines zonal resiliency in the primary region with geo-replication to a secondary region.

questions.scenario: Your team wants a concise, declarative language for Azure infrastructure that compiles to ARM JSON, and the deployment team must avoid switching to a general-purpose scripting tool for the template authoring step.
questions.stem: Which language should you use?
questions.subtopic: Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep files
questions.hint: Concise declarative language that compiles to ARM JSON: what is Azure's domain-specific IaC language?

options.rationale: PowerShell can automate deployments but is not the declarative language that compiles to ARM JSON.
Bicep is the Azure-native domain-specific language that transpiles to ARM JSON.
KQL is used for querying logs, not defining infrastructure deployments.
Azure Resource Manager deployments are not authored as XML.

questions.explanation: Bicep is the concise declarative language designed for Azure deployments and compiles into ARM template JSON.

questions.scenario: You need a starting ARM template that reflects resources already deployed in a resource group, but you do not want to rebuild the template manually or capture unrelated subscriptions. The exported template must help you preserve the current design without starting from scratch.
questions.stem: Which Azure capability should you use?
questions.subtopic: Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep files
questions.referenceTopic: Export a deployment as an Azure Resource Manager template
questions.hint: Starting point from existing infrastructure: which portal feature exports deployed resources as a template?

options.text: Export template from the resource group
options.rationale: Export template captures the current resource configuration as ARM JSON.
Remediation fixes policy drift but does not export deployment artifacts.
Backups preserve workload data, not infrastructure definitions.
Bastion provides secure remote access and does not export templates.

questions.explanation: Export template is the portal feature used to generate an ARM template from existing Azure resources.

questions.scenario: A business-critical virtual machine must remain available if one datacenter in the region fails. The region supports availability zones, and the deployment must protect the workload without requiring a separate regional redesign.
questions.stem: How should you deploy the virtual machine?
questions.referenceTopic: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and availability sets
questions.hint: Datacenter-level failure protection within ONE region: which availability construct provides zonal separation?

options.rationale: Availability sets protect inside a datacenter boundary and do not provide zonal separation.
Availability zones place compute in physically separate datacenters within the region.
Dedicated hosts isolate physical servers but do not inherently provide zonal resiliency.
ACI is a container service and not a virtual machine deployment option.

questions.explanation: Availability zones are the right choice when you need protection against a datacenter-level outage in a supported region.

questions.scenario: You plan to move VM1 to another resource group in the same subscription by using the Azure portal move operation, and the move must keep the workload consistent without breaking attached dependencies.
questions.stem: What should you include in the move request with the virtual machine?
questions.referenceTopic: Move a virtual machine to another resource group, subscription, or region
questions.hint: VM dependencies must move together: which resources (NICs, disks) need to travel WITH the VM?

options.rationale: A VM move usually requires its dependent resources such as NICs and disks to move together.

options.text: The virtual machine and its dependent resources
options.rationale: Dependent resources must be included so the move remains consistent and valid.
The disk alone is insufficient because the VM depends on more than just storage.
Resource groups themselves are not moved; resources are moved between them.

questions.explanation: VM moves typically require you to move the virtual machine together with the dependent NIC and storage resources.

questions.scenario: A security baseline requires encryption of the temporary disk and host cache for supported Azure virtual machines while leaving guest-level data protection unchanged. The control must cover supported VM sizes without relying only on in-guest encryption.
questions.stem: Which feature should you enable?
questions.referenceTopic: Configure encryption at host for Azure virtual machines
questions.hint: Encrypt temp disk AND host cache at the HOST level (not just guest OS): which encryption feature covers both?

options.rationale: Azure Disk Encryption protects OS and data disks in-guest, but not the host cache and temporary disk requirement stated here.

options.text: Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys only
options.rationale: Server-side encryption at rest does not satisfy the host cache and temporary disk requirement.
Encryption at host specifically covers the host cache and temporary disk on supported VM sizes.

options.text: BitLocker inside the guest OS only
options.rationale: Guest OS encryption alone does not provide host-level encryption coverage.

questions.explanation: Encryption at host is the Azure feature specifically intended to encrypt the host cache and temporary disk for supported virtual machines.

questions.scenario: A SQL Server virtual machine needs high and predictable disk performance, but it does not need the specific sub-millisecond latency profile of Ultra disks. The storage choice must support production workloads without adding unnecessary complexity.
questions.stem: Which managed disk type should you choose?
questions.hint: High, predictable performance for SQL Server (not Ultra-class latency requirement): which disk type is standard for production VMs?

options.rationale: Standard HDD is the lowest-cost option and is not suitable for high, predictable performance.
Standard SSD improves latency but is not the best fit for the stated performance requirement.
Premium SSD is the common choice for high-performance VM workloads that do not require Ultra Disk behavior.
Ephemeral OS disk is a deployment choice for stateless OS disks, not a persistent high-performance data disk option.

questions.explanation: Premium SSD is the standard choice for production VM workloads that need strong and predictable disk performance short of Ultra Disk requirements.

questions.scenario: A web tier must run across identical VM instances and automatically scale from 2 to 10 instances based on CPU utilization. The team wants scale-out behavior without redesigning the application for a different hosting model.
questions.stem: Which Azure compute resource should you deploy?
questions.referenceTopic: Deploy and configure an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
questions.hint: Identical instances with automatic scaling 2-10 based on CPU: which compute resource provides both uniform deployment and autoscale?

options.rationale: Availability sets improve resiliency for a fixed set of VMs but do not provide built-in autoscale.
VM scale sets are designed for identical instances with autoscale support.
Dedicated hosts allocate physical servers and do not provide scale-out behavior by themselves.
A Recovery Services vault provides backup and disaster recovery, not VM execution or scaling.

questions.explanation: Virtual machine scale sets are the Azure-native construct for managing identical VM instances with autoscale behavior.

questions.scenario: A data processing pipeline must run a containerized batch task for 30 minutes daily without managing servers, clusters, or paying for idle compute time. Cost efficiency is critical since this runs across multiple time zones.
questions.stem: Which service should you use?
questions.subtopic: Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal
questions.referenceTopic: Provision a container by using Azure Container Instances
questions.hint: 30-minute daily batch, no server management, no idle charges: which serverless container service runs once and stops?

options.rationale: ACI is built for simple container execution without managing infrastructure.
AKS is more operationally heavy than required for a short single-container task.
Azure Backup protects workloads and does not run containers.
Bastion provides secure remote access and is unrelated to container execution.

questions.explanation: Azure Container Instances are appropriate for quickly running containerized workloads without cluster management overhead.

questions.scenario: A containerized HTTP microservice needs revision support, automatic scaling, and the ability to scale to zero when idle. The platform team must keep the service managed without taking on Kubernetes operations.
questions.stem: Which Azure service should you use?
questions.subtopic: Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal
questions.referenceTopic: Provision a container by using Azure Container Apps
questions.hint: HTTP microservice with revisions, autoscale, scale-to-zero, managed platform: which service provides ALL these?

options.rationale: ACR stores images but does not execute containerized web services.
ACI can run containers, but Container Apps is the better fit for HTTP ingress, revisions, and scale-to-zero.
Container Apps is designed for managed containerized applications with revisions and scale-to-zero.
Site Recovery is for disaster recovery, not application hosting.

questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps best matches the requirement for HTTP-based container apps with managed scaling, revisions, and scale-to-zero behavior.

questions.scenario: Your developers need a private Azure service to store and manage container images without publishing those images to a public registry.
questions.stem: Which service should you deploy?
questions.subtopic: Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal
questions.referenceTopic: Create and manage an Azure Container Registry
questions.hint: Private container image storage in Azure: what is the purpose-built service for managing your organization's images?

options.rationale: ACR is the private container image registry service for Azure.
App Service hosts applications but is not an image registry.
Azure Monitor collects telemetry and does not store images.
Azure DNS hosts DNS zones and is unrelated to container images.

questions.explanation: Azure Container Registry is the correct private service for storing and managing container images.

questions.scenario: An App Service app must be reachable by the existing subdomain app.contoso.com. The DNS change must work without moving the app to a different hosting platform or requiring SSL/TLS certificate redirection complications.
questions.stem: Which DNS record type is commonly used for this App Service custom domain mapping?
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Map an existing custom DNS name to an App Service
questions.hint: Map subdomain to App Service: which DNS record type creates an alias to the app's default hostname?

options.rationale: PTR records are used for reverse DNS lookups.
SRV records describe service endpoints and are not the standard choice here.
CNAME is commonly used for mapping an App Service subdomain to the app's default hostname.
MX records are used for mail routing, not web app hostname mapping.

questions.explanation: A CNAME record is the common choice when mapping a subdomain to an App Service hostname.

questions.scenario: You need to deploy a new App Service version, warm it up, validate it, and then move production traffic with minimal downtime. The release process must let you test the new build while keeping the live site available, while avoiding a direct cutover that would increase outage risk.
questions.stem: Which App Service feature should you use?
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure deployment slots for an App Service
questions.hint: Staged validation + low-downtime traffic swap: which App Service feature enables blue-green releases?

options.rationale: Deployment slots support staged validation and controlled cutover with minimal downtime.
Stopping the app increases downtime and removes the warm-up benefit.
Backup restore is for recovery and not the normal release mechanism.
Scaling up changes compute size but does not stage and swap application versions.

questions.explanation: Deployment slots are designed for low-downtime App Service releases and support warming and validation before swap.

questions.scenario: A web app must automatically scale out based on CPU usage, and the business wants the smallest plan tier that supports autoscale without paying for a higher tier than necessary.
questions.stem: What is the minimum App Service plan tier that supports this requirement?
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure scaling for an App Service plan
questions.hint: Minimum tier supporting autoscale (not Free/Shared/Basic): which tier unlocks scaling?

options.rationale: Free does not support autoscale.
Shared does not support autoscale.
Basic supports manual scale but not autoscale.
Standard is the first commonly used tier that supports autoscale features.

questions.explanation: Standard and higher App Service plan tiers support autoscale, whereas Free, Shared, and Basic do not.

questions.scenario: Your team is standardizing on Bicep for Azure infrastructure automation and must explain it clearly to developers who are used to ARM JSON templates. The team must understand what Bicep does and what it does not replace.
questions.stem: Which two statements about Bicep are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep files
questions.hint: Bicep facts: Does it compile to ARM JSON? Does it support resource group deployments? Or does it replace RBAC/KQL?

options.text: Bicep files compile to ARM template JSON
options.rationale: Bicep transpiles into ARM JSON before deployment.

options.text: Bicep files can be deployed at the resource group scope
options.rationale: Bicep supports deployment to resource groups and other scopes.

options.text: Bicep replaces RBAC role assignments entirely
options.rationale: RBAC still exists and is not replaced by Bicep.

options.text: Bicep is used to query Azure Monitor logs
options.rationale: KQL is used for querying logs, not Bicep.

questions.explanation: Bicep is a deployment authoring language that compiles to ARM JSON and supports resource-group-scope deployments.

questions.scenario: You want Azure Container Apps to pull images from a private Azure Container Registry without using registry admin credentials. The solution must remain passwordless and cannot expose the registry to anonymous pulls.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Provision and manage containers in the Azure portal
questions.referenceTopic: Create and manage an Azure Container Registry and provision Azure Container Apps
questions.hint: Passwordless container auth: managed identity + AcrPull role for pulling images from private ACR.

options.text: Configure the container app to authenticate to the registry by using a managed identity
options.rationale: Managed identity is the preferred passwordless pattern for registry access from Container Apps.

options.text: Grant the managed identity the AcrPull role on the registry
options.rationale: AcrPull is the registry permission that allows image pulls without admin credentials.

options.text: Enable anonymous pull on the registry
options.rationale: Anonymous pull weakens security and is unnecessary for this requirement.
Route tables do not grant registry authorization.

questions.explanation: The correct secure pattern is to use a managed identity and grant it AcrPull on the registry.

questions.scenario: You want to reduce risk during App Service releases by validating a new build before users receive it. The release process must support a safe pre-production check and a low-downtime cutover without deploying straight to production.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure deployment slots for an App Service
questions.hint: Safe release pattern: isolate new version BEFORE production → test it → swap when ready. Which slot + which action?

options.rationale: A staging slot gives you an isolated location for validation before production swap.

options.text: Deploy the new build directly to production
options.rationale: Direct production deployment removes the safe validation stage.

options.text: Swap the validated slot into production
options.rationale: Swapping after validation is the standard low-downtime release step.
The production slot is required and should not be deleted.

questions.explanation: Deployment slots reduce release risk by letting you validate in staging and then swap into production.

questions.scenario: Before a risky App Service release, the operations team wants a backup they can restore if needed, while keeping the app on a supported tier and preserving a restore target outside the app itself.
questions.stem: Which two conditions or actions are required? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure backup for an App Service
questions.hint: App Service backup prerequisites: plan tier must SUPPORT backups + external storage to HOLD backups. Which two?

options.text: Use an App Service plan that supports backups, such as Standard or higher
options.rationale: Backups require a plan tier that supports the feature.

options.text: Configure a storage account container for the backup target
options.rationale: App Service backups write to an Azure Storage account.

options.text: Enable Azure Site Recovery on the app
options.rationale: Site Recovery does not provide App Service backup functionality.

options.text: Move the app to the Free tier
options.rationale: Free tier does not support backups.

questions.explanation: App Service backups require a supporting plan tier and a storage destination to hold the backup artifacts.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing statements about compute services in Azure before approving a deployment standard, and the team must avoid incorrect guidance that would affect autoscaling, container hosting, or release workflows.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.subtopic: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
questions.referenceTopic: Create and configure virtual machines, containers, and App Service
questions.hint: Compute services: VM scale sets can auto-scale; ACI works without requiring ACR; deployment slots reduce downtime.

statements.text: Virtual machine scale sets can automatically add instances based on autoscale rules.
Azure Container Instances require Azure Container Registry for every deployment.
Deployment slot swaps can reduce downtime during App Service releases.

questions.explanation: VM scale sets support autoscale, ACI can use images from other supported registries, and deployment slots help reduce release downtime.

questions.scenario: You are validating high-availability and container statements for an architecture review, and the design must support regional resilience and host-level encryption without introducing incorrect platform assumptions.
questions.stem: For each statement, answer Yes if the statement is correct. Otherwise, answer No.
questions.referenceTopic: Deploy virtual machines to availability zones and configure encryption at host
questions.hint: HA & encryption: zones protect datacenters; encryption at host covers temp disk/cache; ACR stores both Linux AND Windows.

statements.text: Availability zones protect virtual machines from a datacenter-level failure within a region.
Encryption at host encrypts the temporary disk and host cache for supported virtual machines.
Azure Container Registry can store only Linux images.

questions.explanation: Availability zones are zonal resiliency boundaries, encryption at host covers temp disk and cache, and ACR can store both Linux and Windows container images.

questions.scenario: You are deploying a new environment from a Bicep file at the resource group scope. The team must keep the rollout repeatable, validate parameter overrides for cost estimation before applying them, and avoid manual cleanup after each deployment.
questions.stem: Arrange the actions in the correct order so the deployment succeeds without manual cleanup or unexpected costs.
questions.subtopic: Automate deployment of resources by using Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep files
questions.referenceTopic: Deploy resources by using a Bicep file
questions.hint: Bicep workflow: Target must EXIST first → VALIDATE before deploying → DEPLOY → REVIEW. What is the correct sequence?
availableItems: Validate the Bicep template with parameters
correctOrder: Validate the Bicep template with parameters
questions.explanation: The target scope must exist first, then validate the template to catch errors and cost overruns before deployment, deploy, and finally review outputs to confirm expected results.

questions.scenario: You are preparing a blue-green release for an App Service that supports a customer portal used during business hours. Operations must keep the live site online while the new build is validated in isolation, and the team must preserve a rollback path if smoke tests fail before any production traffic is switched.
questions.stem: Arrange the actions in the correct order so validation happens before production traffic is swapped.
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure deployment slots for an App Service
questions.hint: Blue-green release: First create slot BEFORE deploying → deploy to isolated slot → swap ONLY after validation.
availableItems: Deploy the new build to the staging slot
Swap the staging slot into production
correctOrder: Deploy the new build to the staging slot
Swap the staging slot into production
questions.explanation: A proper slot-based release creates or uses a staging slot, deploys there, and swaps only after validation is complete.

questions.scenario: You are editing an App Service app in the Azure portal and must require clients to use TLS 1.2 or newer while leaving the rest of the app configuration unchanged.
questions.stem: Which setting should you change?
questions.subtopic: Create and configure Azure App Service
questions.referenceTopic: Configure certificates and Transport Layer Security (TLS) for an App Service
questions.hint: Enforce TLS 1.2 minimum: which App Service setting controls minimum accepted TLS protocol version?

options.rationale: This is the App Service setting that enforces the minimum accepted TLS protocol version.
ARR Affinity controls session stickiness, not TLS version enforcement.
Always On keeps the app warm but does not set TLS requirements.
Platform bitness selects 32-bit or 64-bit runtime behavior, not TLS behavior.

questions.explanation: The Minimum TLS Version setting is the correct place to enforce a TLS 1.2 baseline for App Service.

questions.scenario: Two Azure virtual networks in the same region must communicate privately with low latency over the Microsoft backbone.
questions.stem: Which feature should you use?
questions.subtopic: Configure and manage virtual networks in Azure
questions.referenceTopic: Create and configure virtual network peering
questions.hint: Private IP connectivity between two VNets over Azure backbone: which VNet-to-VNet feature enables this?

options.rationale: VNet peering provides private IP connectivity between Azure virtual networks over the Azure backbone.
A load balancer distributes traffic and does not connect two virtual networks together.
Recovery vaults are for backup and disaster recovery.
Policy enforces governance and does not create network connectivity.

questions.explanation: Virtual network peering is the Azure-native feature for private connectivity between VNets.

questions.scenario: All outbound traffic from Subnet-App must pass through a firewall virtual machine at 10.0.0.4 while keeping the subnet isolated from direct internet egress.
questions.stem: Which Azure networking feature should you configure?
questions.subtopic: Configure and manage virtual networks in Azure
questions.hint: Force traffic through firewall appliance: what routing feature defines next-hop as a virtual appliance?

options.text: A route table with a custom route
options.rationale: User-defined routes in a route table let you send traffic to a virtual appliance.
ASGs group NICs for NSG rules and do not define routing paths.
A public IP alone does not direct subnet traffic through a firewall.
Azure DNS resolves names and does not control next-hop routing.

questions.explanation: A route table with a custom next hop to a virtual appliance is the standard way to steer subnet traffic through a firewall VM.

questions.scenario: A VM cannot receive traffic that you believe an NSG should allow. You must verify the combined rules that are actually applied to the VM's NIC without guessing which rule set is winning.
questions.stem: Which Azure tool or view should you use?
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.referenceTopic: Evaluate effective security rules in NSGs
questions.hint: NSG troubleshooting: what diagnostic view shows the FINAL merged NSG behavior on a NIC?

options.rationale: The effective security rules view shows the resulting NSG behavior on the NIC.
Advisor does not show the merged NSG decision path for a NIC.
Budgets do not help troubleshoot packet filtering.
Locks protect resources from changes and do not show packet filtering.

questions.explanation: Effective security rules are the right diagnostic view when you need to understand the final NSG behavior on a network interface.

questions.scenario: Administrators must connect to Azure virtual machines over RDP and SSH without exposing those VMs with public IP addresses. Audit and compliance teams must be able to review access logs for the administrative sessions.
questions.stem: Which service should you deploy?
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.hint: Secure admin access without public IPs on VMs: which managed service provides browser-based RDP/SSH?

options.rationale: Azure Bastion provides browser-based RDP and SSH to VMs without public IPs on the VM NICs.
Azure DNS hosts DNS records and does not provide remote access.

options.text: A jump host VM with a public IP
options.rationale: A jump host VM can provide access but requires a public IP on the VM, violating the no-public-IP requirement.
Recovery vaults do not provide interactive VM access.

questions.explanation: Azure Bastion is purpose-built for secure management access to Azure VMs without public IP exposure; it provides browser-based RDP/SSH access and audit logging without placing public IPs on the VMs themselves.

questions.scenario: Subnet-App must reach an Azure Storage account over the Azure backbone while the storage account continues to use its public endpoint. The design must keep the public endpoint in place without exposing the storage account to every network.
questions.stem: Which feature should you configure?
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.referenceTopic: Configure service endpoints for Azure platform as a service (PaaS)
questions.hint: Keep PUBLIC endpoint, enable private path from subnet: what extends VNet identity to PaaS over Azure backbone?

options.rationale: Service endpoints keep the PaaS public endpoint but extend VNet identity to it over the Azure backbone.
A private endpoint assigns a private IP to the service connection instead of using the public endpoint.
ASGs categorize NICs for NSG rules and do not connect to PaaS services.
A public IP prefix allocates public addresses and does not solve subnet-to-PaaS connectivity.

questions.explanation: Service endpoints extend a subnet's identity to reach a PaaS service's public endpoint over the Azure backbone, allowing private connectivity without exposing the PaaS service to every network on the internet; private endpoints use a different mechanism (private IP inside your VNet) and are a separate feature for different scenarios.

questions.scenario: An Azure SQL Database must be reachable only over a private IP address from an application subnet, and the solution must avoid using the public internet path.
questions.stem: Which feature should you configure?
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.referenceTopic: Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
questions.hint: Private IP-only access to PaaS (no public path): what creates a private IP endpoint inside your VNet?

options.rationale: Service endpoints do not place a private IP for the PaaS service into your VNet.
Private endpoints map the service connection to a private IP in your VNet.
A route table cannot create private service connectivity on its own.
A public load balancer exposes services to the internet and is not needed here.

questions.explanation: Private endpoints are the correct feature when a PaaS service must be reachable over a private IP from your virtual network.

questions.scenario: Your company must use Microsoft-hosted authoritative DNS for the public internet domain contoso.com without delegating the zone to a third-party DNS provider.
questions.stem: Which service should you use?
questions.subtopic: Configure name resolution and load balancing
questions.hint: Host authoritative public DNS zone in Azure: which Microsoft service provides DNS zone hosting?

options.rationale: Azure DNS hosts authoritative public and private DNS zones in Azure.
Private DNS zones are for internal name resolution and do not host a public internet domain.
Traffic Manager is a DNS-based load balancer for routing user traffic, not for hosting authoritative DNS zones.
Policy does not provide DNS hosting.

questions.explanation: Azure DNS is the Azure service used to host authoritative DNS zones for public domains such as contoso.com.

questions.scenario: Two web virtual machines must receive inbound TCP 443 traffic from the internet by using a single Azure frontend IP. TLS offload is not required, and the platform must stay at layer 4 rather than adding an application gateway.
questions.stem: Which Azure service should you deploy?
questions.subtopic: Configure name resolution and load balancing
questions.referenceTopic: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.hint: Internet-facing L4 traffic distribution to VMs: which load balancer SKU supports public frontend IP?

options.rationale: A public load balancer can distribute inbound TCP traffic from a public frontend IP to backend virtual machines.
An internal load balancer is private and not reachable from the internet.
An ASG groups NICs for NSG rules and does not distribute traffic.
Route tables define routing and do not provide inbound load distribution.

questions.explanation: A public Azure Load Balancer is the correct choice for L4 traffic distribution from a public frontend IP to Azure VMs.

questions.scenario: An internal line-of-business application must be load balanced only for clients inside the virtual network and connected on-premises networks. The service must remain private while still allowing shared access across internal consumers.
questions.stem: Which load-balancing option should you use?
questions.subtopic: Configure name resolution and load balancing
questions.referenceTopic: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.hint: Private load balancing for internal users only: which LB keeps frontend IP private and non-internet-facing?

options.rationale: An internal load balancer exposes a private frontend IP for internal consumers only.
A public load balancer exposes a public frontend IP to internet clients.
A public IP prefix allocates addresses and does not itself balance traffic.
A storage firewall controls storage access and is unrelated to application load balancing.

questions.explanation: An internal load balancer is the correct choice when the service should stay private and reachable only across internal networks.

questions.scenario: A backend VM in a Standard Load Balancer pool is always reported unhealthy after a subnet NSG was tightened for a production change freeze. The team must restore probe health without broadly opening inbound traffic to the application port or weakening the subnet's general protection, while still keeping the backend protected from unrelated client traffic.
questions.stem: Which NSG rule is most likely missing if you want the backend to stay protected?
questions.subtopic: Configure name resolution and load balancing
questions.hint: Unhealthy backend after NSG tightening: health probes originate from which Azure service that must be allowed?

options.text: An inbound allow rule from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag
options.rationale: Health probes originate from AzureLoadBalancer and the backend can remain unhealthy if that traffic is blocked.

options.text: An outbound deny rule to the Internet service tag
options.rationale: Outbound deny rules do not directly fix inbound health probe failures.

options.text: An inbound allow rule from the VirtualNetwork service tag only
options.rationale: VirtualNetwork alone does not specifically allow the Azure load balancer probe source.
Routing is not the first missing control indicated by a blocked health probe.

questions.explanation: If the AzureLoadBalancer service tag is blocked by NSG rules, health probes cannot reach the backend instance and the load balancer marks it unhealthy.

questions.scenario: You are deploying a Standard public load balancer and want a resilient public IP that is explicitly allocated and retained. The frontend must keep the same address across service updates without relying on dynamic allocation.
questions.stem: Which public IP configuration should you choose?
questions.subtopic: Configure and manage virtual networks in Azure
questions.hint: Standard LB with persistent IP: which SKU + allocation type keeps the same address?

options.rationale: Basic is not aligned with the Standard load balancer requirement and dynamic addressing can change.
Standard public IPs are used with Standard load balancers and should be static for a fixed frontend address.
Basic is the wrong SKU pairing for a Standard load balancer.
A public load balancer frontend needs a public IP when it must be internet facing.

questions.explanation: A Standard Load Balancer should use a Standard SKU public IP, and static allocation preserves the address.

questions.scenario: A storage account uses a private endpoint. Virtual machines in VNet-App must resolve the storage account FQDN to the private endpoint address, and the DNS configuration must work without exposing the service to the public internet.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.referenceTopic: Configure private endpoints for Azure PaaS
questions.hint: Private endpoint DNS: create zone HOLDING records + link zone TO VNet. Which two?

options.text: Create the appropriate private DNS zone for the private endpoint service
options.rationale: Private DNS zones provide the internal records that map the service FQDN to the private endpoint IP.

options.text: Link the private DNS zone to VNet-App
options.rationale: The consuming VNet must be linked so clients there use the private records.
Flow logs do not create DNS records or resolution behavior.

options.text: Create a public IP address for the private endpoint
options.rationale: Private endpoints use private IPs and do not need public IPs.

questions.explanation: Private endpoint name resolution requires the correct private DNS zone (which holds the DNS records) and a VNet link (which makes those records resolvable from the consuming network). Without the VNet link, records exist but are invisible to clients in the VNet.

questions.scenario: An NSG design is becoming hard to manage across many web and database servers. You want to reduce rule maintenance, target rules at groups of NICs, and keep the design maintainable as new workloads are added without rewriting every rule set or duplicating the same allow rules in each NSG.
questions.stem: Which two features must you use to reduce rule maintenance without duplicating the same logic in every NSG? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
questions.subtopic: Configure secure access to virtual networks
questions.referenceTopic: Create and configure network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups
questions.hint: Reduce NSG duplication: use ASGs to target groups of NICs, use service tags for Azure services. Which two?

options.rationale: ASGs let you target NSG rules at logical groups of NICs.
Service tags simplify rules that target Azure service address ranges.
Recovery Services vaults are unrelated to packet filtering design.
Management groups organize subscriptions and do not simplify individual NSG rules.

questions.explanation: Application security groups simplify NSG rules between your own resources by allowing you to target groups of NICs without rewriting every rule; service tags simplify rules for Azure-managed services because Microsoft automatically updates the IP ranges when services change their public endpoints.

questions.scenario: Outbound traffic from Subnet-App must pass through a firewall VM at 10.0.0.4, and the route must take effect without forcing a redesign of the subnet layout.

options.text: Create a public IP for every VM in the subnet

questions.scenario: You are reviewing basic Azure networking statements for a foundation-level design review, and the team must avoid mixing up private connectivity, admin access, and route behavior.

A public IP address is required on a VM that is accessed through Azure Bastion.
A user-defined route can direct traffic to a virtual appliance.

questions.scenario: You are checking secure PaaS connectivity and load balancer troubleshooting statements for a production review. The design must preserve private connectivity while still allowing you to diagnose unhealthy backends without weakening access controls.

questions.scenario: You are deploying an Azure Load Balancer for an internal application. The health probe must be configured to detect backend failures within 30 seconds, and the rule must tie everything together so traffic is routed only to healthy backends.

questions.scenario: A virtual machine in a subnet cannot reach a remote endpoint during an incident review. questions.scenario: You need an alert when the Percentage CPU metric on a virtual machine stays above 80 percent for 10 minutes so the operations team can respond before user impact increases and without relying on a cost-based alert.

questions.referenceTopic: Configure log settings in Azure Monitor
questions.hint: For centralized KQL queries across Azure Monitor logs, choose the dedicated log analytics data store.

Application Insights is specialized for app-level telemetry and diagnostics, not general Azure Monitor logs.
Azure DNS resolves names and does not provide log storage or querying.
Bastion secures VM access and is unrelated to log storage.

questions.explanation: Log Analytics workspaces are the core data store for Azure Monitor logs and KQL-based analysis; Application Insights is for application-specific telemetry, not general operational logs.

questions.scenario: An alert rule is correct, but notifications should be suppressed automatically during a planned maintenance window while leaving the underlying alert definition intact and without disabling the rule itself.

questions.hint: You need to suppress notifications during maintenance without changing alert detection logic.

Locks do not control alert notification pipelines.
